Date: February 10 2009
Abstract.

In this paper, we give a systematic construction of ten isomonodromic families of connections of rank two on ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1} inducing Painlevé equations. The classification of ten families is given by considering the Riemann-Hilbert morphism from a moduli space of connections with certain type of regular and irregular singularities to a corresponding catetorical moduli space of analytic data (i.e., ordinary monodromy, Stokes matrices and links), which is called the monodromy space. Explicit equations of the monodromy spaces for ten families are calculated. Moreover, we obtain natural explicit families of connections for these ten cases and calculate isomonodromic equations which give Painlevé equations of all types.

Key words and phrases: 
Moduli space for linear connections, Irregular singularities, Stokes matrices, Monodromy spaces, Isomonodromic deformations, Painlevé equations
1991 Mathematics Subject Classification
14D20,14D25,34M55,58F05

Introduction

The theme of this paper is a systematic construction of the ten isomonodromic families of connections of rank two on ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1} inducing Painlevé equations. They are obtained by considering the complex analytic Riemann–Hilbert morphism R​H:ℳ→ℛRH:\mathcal{M}\rightarrow\mathcal{R} from a moduli space ℳ\mathcal{M} of connections to a categorical moduli space of analytic data (i.e., ordinary monodromy, Stokes matrices and links) ℛ\mathcal{R}, here called the monodromy space. The fibres of R​HRH are the isomonodromic families. One requires that an isomonodromic family has dimension 1, since it is then (locally) parametrized by one variable tt and some combination q⁡(t)q(t) of the entries of the connection is a potential solution of some second order Painlevé equation. This condition leads to the ten families. Our method extends the work of Jimbo, Miwa and Ueno, [JMU, JM].

There is a natural morphism ℛ→𝒫\mathcal{R}\rightarrow\mathcal{P}, where 𝒫\mathcal{P} is a parameter space build from traces of matrices. For each of the ten families, the morphism ℛ→𝒫\mathcal{R}\rightarrow\mathcal{P} turns out to be a family of affine cubic surfaces with three lines at infinity. We will give explicit equations of ℛ\mathcal{R} for these ten families in §2 and §3. The equation for Painlevé VI is classical [FK, Iw2], and other equations for nine families seem to be new. (See Table 2).

Since many aspects of the well known family with four regular singularities leading to Painlevé VI, has been studied in great detail ([Boa, IIS1, IIS2, IISA, Iw2]), our emphasis will be on families with irregular singularities. Of the nine families with irregular singularities, six are again classical [JM, FN]. The three ‘new’ ones were also recently discovered in [OO, OKSO, Sakai].

The moduli spaces of connections ℳ\mathcal{M} are strongly related to the Okamoto–Painlevé pairs (S,Y)(S,Y) of non fibre type. Although this is not the theme of this paper, we will give a brief description of this relation, since it gives an heuristic idea of the meaning of the ten types of isomonodromic families.

The surface SS is the blow up of nine points (allowing for infinitely near points) in ℙ2\mathbb{P}^{2} (or equivalently eight points in the Hirzebruch surface Σ2\Sigma_{2}) which lie on an effective anti-canonical divisor of ℙ2\mathbb{P}^{2} or Σ2\Sigma_{2}. Let YY be the unique effective anti-canonical divisor of SS. The Okamoto–Painelevé condition on YY implies that YY has the same configuration as a degenerate elliptic curve in the classification by Kodaira–Néron [O1, Sakai, STT].

The configuration of the irreducible components of YY for the Okamoto–Painlevé pairs are given by the eight extended Dynkin diagrams

D~4,D~5,D~6,D~7,D~8,E~6,E~7,E~8.\tilde{D}_{4},\tilde{D}_{5},\tilde{D}_{6},\tilde{D}_{7},\tilde{D}_{8},\ \tilde{E}_{6},\ \tilde{E}_{7},\ \tilde{E}_{8}.

One conjectures that each of (uni)versal global families of the eight types of Okamoto–Painlevé pairs can be constructed as a moduli space of connections π:ℳ→T×Λ\pi:\mathcal{M}\rightarrow T\times\Lambda with parameter space T×ΛT\times\Lambda. The fibres of π\pi are the complement S∖YS\setminus Y for a certain Okamoto–Painlevé pair (S,Y)(S,Y) of the given type, related to Painlevé equations.

The conjecture has been proven for Okamoto–Painlevé pair of type D~4\tilde{D}_{4}, which corresponds to Painlevé VI. (For the construction of the moduli spaces of linear connections with only regular singularities and the Riemann-Hilbert correspondence for these, see [IIS1, IIS2, In].)

There is an explicit analytic morphism Λ→𝒫\Lambda\rightarrow\mathcal{P}, given by exponentials, which is compatible with the Riemann–Hilbert morphism R​H:ℳ→ℛRH:\mathcal{M}\rightarrow\mathcal{R}. The monodromy space ℛ→𝒫\mathcal{R}\rightarrow\mathcal{P} can have, as fibre, a singular (affine) cubic surface. The Riemann–Hilbert morphism yields an analytic resolution, namely an Okamoto–Painlevé space S∖YS\setminus Y, of this singular cubic surface. The singular points of type A1,A2,A3,D4A_{1},A_{2},A_{3},D_{4} on the cubic surface yield 1, 2, 3 and 4 exceptional curves on (S,Y)(S,Y) which are called Riccati curves. The latter are related to Riccati solutions of the corresponding Painlevé equation. Since the Riccati curves on the Okamoto–Painlevé pairs are known ([STe]), one can now link each of the ten monodromy spaces ℛ\mathcal{R} to an Okamoto–Painlevé pair and an extended Dynkin diagram (see Table 1). We remark, as done in [OO], that for the case D~6\tilde{D}_{6} there are two types of isomonodromic families which correspond to deg PV and PIII(D6D_{6}). The (uni)versal property might imply that the two types are analytically isomorphic. The same remark holds for E~7\tilde{E}_{7}.

The contents of this paper is the following. The first section deals with the formal and analytic data attached to a differential module MM over ℂ⁡(z)\mathbb{C}(z). The connections on ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1} inducing given formal and analytic data are studied. A weak and a strong form of the Riemann-Hilbert problem is treated. This result is also obtained by [BMM] in a slightly different setting.

In Section 2, ‘good’ families of connections on ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1} are described and studied. The monodromy space ℛ\mathcal{R} is defined as a categorical quotient of the analytic data.

Then the ten families where the fibres of R​H:ℳ→ℛRH:\mathcal{M}\rightarrow\mathcal{R} have dimension 1 are computed. The third Section contains the computation of the ten monodromy spaces ℛ→𝒫\mathcal{R}\rightarrow\mathcal{P} and the singularities of the fibres.

A theory of apparent singularities qq is developed in Section 4. This is essential for the computation of the second order equation q′′=R⁡(q,q′,t)q^{\prime\prime}=R(q,q^{\prime},t) (where RR is a rational function of q′,q,tq^{\prime},q,t) of the Painlevé type and of a corresponding symplectic structure with canonical coordinates p,qp,q and a Hamiltonian equation. We obtain explicit Hamiltonian systems and explicit Painlevé equations for the nine families (see Subsections 4.3–4.11) which are natural form the view point of the Okamoto–Painlevé pairs. The explicit forms of equations depend on the choice of a cyclic vector, the choice of the parameter tt and choices for the constants in the monodromy space. Though we will not tune up these data such that our explicit forms coincide with the classical Painlevé equations as in [Gam, P, JM], one can transform one to the another by some birational transformations of coordinates.

1. Singularities of a differential module

1.1. Summary

Let MM be a differential module over K=ℂ⁡(z)K=\mathbb{C}(z). The formal data (generalized local exponents, formal monodromy), and the analytic data (monodromy, Stokes matrices, links) of MM are described. The weak form of the Riemann-Hilbert problem for arbitrary singularities has the positive answer:

Theorem 1.7 For given formal and analytic data, there exists a unique(up to isomorphism) differential module MM inducing these data.

A strong form of the Riemann–Hilbert problem is:

Theorem 1.11 Suppose that MM is irreducible and has at least one (regular or irregular) singular point which is unramified. Then there is a connection (𝒱,∇)(\mathcal{V},\nabla) on ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1} representing MM, such that 𝒱\mathcal{V} is free (i.e., a direct sum of copies of 𝒪ℙ1\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^{1}}) and the poles of the connection ∇\nabla have the minimal order derived from the Katz invariant.

Results concerning invariant lattices are developed for the proof of Theorem 1.11. That the strong Riemann–Hilbert problem has a negative answer if all the singularities of MM are ramified, is shown by two families of examples related to Painlevé equations. Theorem 1.11 extends Bolibruch’s work [BMM] which deals with the case where all singularities are regular singular. For the convenience of the reader, the useful compact way to describe the formal and the analytic singularities of differential modules (see [PS] for more details) is explained in the next subsections. Explicit examples are given which will be used in the calculations for the monodromy spaces and the Painlevé equations.

1.2. The formal classification

This is the classification of differential modules M=(M,δ)M=(M,\delta) over the differential field of the formal Laurent series ℂ⁡((t))\mathbb{C}((t)) (here tt is the local parameter) , due to M. Hukuhara[Hu] and H. Turrittin [Tu]. For notational convenience we will use the derivation t​dd​tt\frac{d}{dt} on ℂ⁡((t))\mathbb{C}((t)). The ℂ\mathbb{C}-linear map δ:M→M\delta:M\rightarrow M has, by definition, the property δ⁡(f​m)=t​d​fd​t⋅m+f⋅δ⁡(m)\delta(fm)=t\frac{df}{dt}\cdot m+f\cdot\delta(m) for f∈ℂ⁡((t)),m∈Mf\in\mathbb{C}((t)),\ m\in M.
The module MM is called regular singular (this includes regular) if there is an invariant lattice Λ⊂M\Lambda\subset M, i.e., Λ⊂M\Lambda\subset M is a free ℂ⁡[[t]]\mathbb{C}[[t]]-submodule containing a basis of MM such that δ⁡(Λ)⊂Λ\delta(\Lambda)\subset\Lambda. A regular singular MM has a basis e1,…,ede_{1},\dots,e_{d} such that the vector space W:=⊕i=1dℂeiW:=\oplus_{i=1}^{d}\mathbb{C}e_{i} is invariant under δ\delta and such that the distinct eigenvalues λ1,…,λs\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{s} (with 1≤s≤d1\leq s\leq d) of δ\delta acting on WW satisfy λi−λj∉ℤ\lambda_{i}-\lambda_{j}\not\in\mathbb{Z} for i≠ji\neq j. Using this basis the operator δ\delta on MM obtains the form t​dd​t+At\frac{d}{dt}+A, where AA is the matrix of δ\delta operating on WW. The λi\lambda_{i} are called the local exponents. These are only unique up to integers. The (formal) monodromy matrix is (up to conjugation) e2​π​i​Ae^{2\pi iA}.

Clearly Λ:=⊕i=1dℂ[[t]]ei\Lambda:=\oplus_{i=1}^{d}\mathbb{C}[[t]]e_{i} is an invariant lattice. The non resonant case is defined by s=ds=d, i.e., the matrix AA is diagonalizable and its eigenvalues λ1,…,λd\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{d} satisfy λi−λj∉ℤ\lambda_{i}-\lambda_{j}\not\in\mathbb{Z} for i≠ji\neq j. In the non resonant case the collection of all invariant lattices is {⊕i=1dℂ[[t]]tniei|n1,…,nd∈ℤ}\{\oplus_{i=1}^{d}\mathbb{C}[[t]]t^{n_{i}}e_{i}\ |\ n_{1},\dots,n_{d}\in\mathbb{Z}\} and the formal monodromy has dd distinct eigenvalues.

The solutions of a regular singular module MM, say, represented in matrix form t​dd​t+At\frac{d}{dt}+A, are vectors vv with (t​dd​t+A)​v=0(t\frac{d}{dt}+A)v=0. One needs the following differential ring extension U​n​i​vr​s:=ℂ⁡((t))​[{ta}a∈ℂ,ℓ]Univ_{rs}:=\mathbb{C}((t))[\{t^{a}\}_{a\in\mathbb{C}},\ell] of ℂ⁡((t))\mathbb{C}((t)) to obtain the vector space VV of all solutions. The symbols ta,ℓt^{a},\ell are defined by the rules ta⋅tb=ta+bt^{a}\cdot t^{b}=t^{a+b}, t1t^{1} coincides with t∈ℂ⁡((t))t\in\mathbb{C}((t)). Further t​dd​t​ta=a​ta,t​dd​t​ℓ=1t\frac{d}{dt}t^{a}=at^{a},\ t\frac{d}{dt}\ell=1. The intuitive meaning of these symbols is rather clear: tat^{a} stands for ea​log⁡te^{a\log t} and ℓ\ell for log⁡t\log t. Because these functions are multivalued, they are replaced by symbols.

Then VV consists of the vectors vv with coordinates in U​n​i​vr​sUniv_{rs} satisfying (t​dd​t+A)​v=0(t\frac{d}{dt}+A)v=0. In other words, V={v∈U​n​i​vr​s⊗ℂ⁡((t))M|δ⁡(v)=0}V=\{v\in Univ_{rs}\otimes_{\mathbb{C}((t))}M\ |\ \delta(v)=0\}. The ring U​n​i​vr​sUniv_{rs} has a ℂ⁡((t))\mathbb{C}((t))-linear differential automorphism γ\gamma, defined by γ​ta=e2​π​i​a​ta,γ​ℓ=ℓ+2​π​i\gamma t^{a}=e^{2\pi ia}t^{a},\ \gamma\ell=\ell+2\pi i. Now γ\gamma induces on automorphism γ⊗i​d\gamma\otimes id on U​n​i​vr​s⊗MUniv_{rs}\otimes M, commuting with δ\delta. Then VV is invariant under γ\gamma and the restriction of γ\gamma to VV, again written as γ\gamma or γV\gamma_{V}, is the formal monodromy. From the pair (V,γV)(V,\gamma_{V}) one recovers the differential module (M,δM)(M,\delta_{M}) as the ℂ⁡((t))\mathbb{C}((t))-vector space of the γ\gamma-invariant elements of U​n​i​vr​s⊗ℂVUniv_{rs}\otimes_{\mathbb{C}}V. On the last space the operator δ\delta is defined by δ⁡(u⊗v)=δ⁡(u)⊗v\delta(u\otimes v)=\delta(u)\otimes v for u∈U​n​i​vr​s,v∈Vu\in Univ_{rs},\ v\in V. The restriction of this δ\delta to MM is the δM\delta_{M}. The above describes an equivalence between the category of the regular singular differential modules and the category of the pairs (V,γ)(V,\gamma) consisting of a finite dimensional vector VV and an γ∈GL⁡(V)\gamma\in{\rm GL}(V). This equivalence respects all constructions of linear algebra, in particular tensor products.

This maybe somewhat abstract way to deal with regular singular differential modules extends to the case of irregular singular differential modules. It greatly simplifies the various classical classification results.

A typical example of an irregular singular module is the one-dimensional module M=ℂ⁡((z))​eM=\mathbb{C}((z))e with δ​e=(a+q)​e\delta e=(a+q)e with q∈t−1​ℂ​[t−1],q≠0,a∈ℂq\in t^{-1}\mathbb{C}[t^{-1}],\ q\neq 0,\ a\in\mathbb{C}. We call a+qa+q the (generalized) local exponent and qq the eigenvalue. One observes that qq is unique and aa is unique up to a shift over an integer.

A more complicated example is the following. For any integer n≥1n\geq 1 we consider the field extension ℂ⁡((t1/n))\mathbb{C}((t^{1/n})) of degree nn and an element a+q∈ℂ+(t−1/nℂ[t−1/n])a+q\in\mathbb{C}+(t^{-1/n}\mathbb{C}[t^{-1/n}]). Then we define the differential module ℂ⁡((t1/n))​e\mathbb{C}((t^{1/n}))e of rank one over ℂ⁡((t1/n))\mathbb{C}((t^{1/n})) by δ⁡(e)=(a+q)​e\delta(e)=(a+q)e. Now MM is equal to this object, seen as a differential module over the field ℂ⁡((t))\mathbb{C}((t)). This module has dimension nn. From these examples and the regular singular differential modules one can build, by constructions of linear algebra, all differential modules. In order to have solutions for all differential modules over ℂ⁡((t))\mathbb{C}((t)) we have to introduce new symbols e⁡(q)e(q) for q∈𝒬:=⋂n≥1t−1/nℂ[t−1/n]q\in\mathcal{Q}:=\bigcap_{n\geq 1}t^{-1/n}\mathbb{C}[t^{-1/n}]. The rules are t​dd​t​e​(q)=q⋅e⁡(q)t\frac{d}{dt}e(q)=q\cdot e(q) and e⁡(q1)​e​(q2)=e⁡(q1+q2)e(q_{1})e(q_{2})=e(q_{1}+q_{2}). One obtains the differential ring extension Univ:=⊕q∈𝒬Univr​s⋅e(q)Univ:=\oplus_{q\in\mathcal{Q}}Univ_{rs}\cdot e(q), equipped with the differential automorphism γ\gamma, extending the γ\gamma on U​n​i​vr​sUniv_{rs} by γ​e​(q)=e⁡(γ​q)\gamma e(q)=e(\gamma q). The meaning of γ⁡(q)\gamma(q) is already defined since γ⁡(ta)=e2​π​i​a​ta\gamma(t^{a})=e^{2\pi ia}t^{a} for any a∈ℂa\in\mathbb{C}. The intuitive meaning of e⁡(q)e(q) is rather evident, namely e∫q​d​tte^{\int q\frac{dt}{t}}. Since the latter is a multivalued function we avoid its use and use the symbol e⁡(q)e(q) instead.

The solution space VV of a differential module MM, say, represented by the matrix equation t​dd​t+At\frac{d}{dt}+A where AA is a d×dd\times d-matrix with coefficients in ℂ⁡((t))\mathbb{C}((t)), is defined as V={v∈(U​n​i​v)d|(t​dd​t+A)​(v)=0}V=\{v\in(Univ)^{d}\ |\ (t\frac{d}{dt}+A)(v)=0\}. In other words V={v∈U​n​i​v⊗ℂ⁡((t))M|δ⁡(v)=0}V=\{v\in Univ\otimes_{\mathbb{C}((t))}M\ |\ \delta(v)=0\}. As before, there is an action of γ\gamma on VV. Moreover VV has a direct sum decomposition V=⊕q∈𝒬VqV=\oplus_{q\in\mathcal{Q}}V_{q} where Vq:={v∈Univr​s⋅e(q)⊗ℂ⁡((t))M|δ(v)=0}V_{q}:=\{v\in Univ_{rs}\cdot e(q)\otimes_{\mathbb{C}((t))}M\ |\ \delta(v)=0\}. As the dimension of VV is finite (equal to dimℂ⁡((t))M\dim_{\mathbb{C}((t))}M), almost all VqV_{q} are 0. Clearly γ⁡(Vq)=Vγ⁡(q)\gamma(V_{q})=V_{\gamma(q)}. Thus we have attached to MM a tuple (V,{Vq},γ)(V,\{V_{q}\},\gamma) consisting of a finite dimensional vector space VV over ℂ\mathbb{C} and subspaces VqV_{q} with V=⊕q∈𝒬VqV=\oplus_{q\in\mathcal{Q}}V_{q} and an element γ∈GL⁡(V)\gamma\in{\rm GL}(V) such that γ⁡(Vq)=Vγ⁡(q)\gamma(V_{q})=V_{\gamma(q)} for all qq. From this tuple one can recover (M,δM)(M,\delta_{M}) as the ℂ⁡((t))\mathbb{C}((t))-vector space of the γ\gamma-invariant elements of ⊕q∈𝒬Univr​s⋅e(−q)⊗ℂVq\oplus_{q\in\mathcal{Q}}Univ_{rs}\cdot e(-q)\otimes_{\mathbb{C}}V_{q}. By definition δ\delta acts as zero on VV and thus induces δM\delta_{M}. In fact, M↦(V,{Vq},γ)M\mapsto(V,\{V_{q}\},\gamma) defines an equivalence of categories commuting with all operations of linear algebra, and in particular with tensor product. Our formal classification is that of the tuples (V,{Vq},γ)(V,\{V_{q}\},\gamma).

The elements qq with Vq≠0V_{q}\neq 0 are called the eigenvalues and γ\gamma, acting on VV, is called the formal monodromy. The Katz invariant r⁡(M)r(M) of MM is the maximum of the degrees in t−1t^{-1} of the eigenvalues qq.

Definition and examples 1.2.

Invariant lattices.
Let the differential module M=(M,δ)M=(M,\delta) have Katz invariant rr and let r+r^{+} denote the smallest integer ≥r\geq r. A free submodule Λ⊂M\Lambda\subset M over ℂ⁡[[t]]\mathbb{C}[[t]], containing a basis of MM is usually called a lattice. We say that Λ\Lambda is an invariant lattice if, moreover tr+​δ​Λ⊂Λt^{r^{+}}\delta\Lambda\subset\Lambda. There exists an invariant lattice, in fact the standard lattice defined in [PS], p. 307 and p. 311, is an invariant lattice. For later use we will compute all invariant lattices for the items of Examples 1.1.

  1. (i)

    If the regular singular module MM is non resonant, then MM has a basis e1,e2e_{1},e_{2} with δ​e1=θ2​e1,δ​e2=−θ2​e2\delta e_{1}=\frac{\theta}{2}e_{1},\ \delta e_{2}=-\frac{\theta}{2}e_{2} and θ∉ℤ\theta\not\in\mathbb{Z}. The notation θ2\frac{\theta}{2} is chosen for historical reasons. The invariant lattices are ℂ⁡[[t]]​tn1​e1+ℂ⁡[[t]]​tn2​e2\mathbb{C}[[t]]t^{n_{1}}e_{1}+\mathbb{C}[[t]]t^{n_{2}}e_{2} for any n1,n2∈ℤn_{1},n_{2}\in\mathbb{Z}.
    A typical resonant case is M=ℂ⁡((t))​e1+ℂ⁡((t))​e2M=\mathbb{C}((t))e_{1}+\mathbb{C}((t))e_{2} with δ​e1=e2,δ​e2=0\delta e_{1}=e_{2},\ \delta e_{2}=0. The invariant lattices are ℂ⁡[[t]]​tn1​e1+ℂ⁡[[t]]​tn2​e2\mathbb{C}[[t]]t^{n_{1}}e_{1}+\mathbb{C}[[t]]t^{n_{2}}e_{2} with n1,n2∈ℤn_{1},n_{2}\in\mathbb{Z} and n1≥n2n_{1}\geq n_{2}.

  2. (ii)

    MM has a basis e1,e2e_{1},e_{2} with δ​e1=(q+a)​e1,δ​e2=−(q+a)​e2\delta e_{1}=(q+a)e_{1},\ \delta e_{2}=-(q+a)e_{2}. In this case r+=rr^{+}=r and the invariant lattices are ℂ⁡[[t]]​tn1​e1+ℂ⁡[[t]]​tn2​e2\mathbb{C}[[t]]t^{n_{1}}e_{1}+\mathbb{C}[[t]]t^{n_{2}}e_{2} for any n1,n2∈ℤn_{1},n_{2}\in\mathbb{Z}.

  3. (iii)

    MM has basis f1,f2f_{1},f_{2} with δ​f1=h​f2,δ​f2=t​h​f1+12​f2\delta f_{1}=hf_{2},\ \delta f_{2}=thf_{1}+\frac{1}{2}f_{2}. Now r+=r+12r^{+}=r+\frac{1}{2}. The invariant lattices are only the lattices tn⋅(ℂ⁡[[t]]​f1+ℂ⁡[[t]]​f2)t^{n}\cdot(\mathbb{C}[[t]]f_{1}+\mathbb{C}[[t]]f_{2}) and tn⋅(ℂ⁡[[t]]​t​f1+ℂ⁡[[t]]​f2)t^{n}\cdot(\mathbb{C}[[t]]tf_{1}+\mathbb{C}[[t]]f_{2}) where n∈ℤn\in\mathbb{Z}.

We omit the easy proofs for (i) and (ii). The proof of case (iii):
Consider the operator Δ=h−1​δ\Delta=h^{-1}\delta on MM. Thus Δ​f1=f2,Δ​f2=t​f1+12​h​f2\Delta f_{1}=f_{2},\ \Delta f_{2}=tf_{1}+\frac{1}{2h}f_{2} and Δ⁡(f​m)=(h−1​t​d​fd​t)⋅m+f⋅Δ⁡(m)\Delta(fm)=(h^{-1}t\frac{df}{dt})\cdot m+f\cdot\Delta(m).

A lattice Λ\Lambda is invariant if and only if Δ​Λ⊂Λ\Delta\Lambda\subset\Lambda. If Λ\Lambda is an invariant lattice then also tn⋅Λt^{n}\cdot\Lambda for any n∈ℤn\in\mathbb{Z}. The lattices generated by f1,f2f_{1},f_{2} and by t​f1,f2tf_{1},f_{2} are clearly invariant. Let Λ\Lambda be any invariant lattice. After multiplication by some power of tt we may suppose that Λ⊂(ℂ⁡[[t]]​f1+ℂ⁡[[t]]​f2)\Lambda\subset(\mathbb{C}[[t]]f_{1}+\mathbb{C}[[t]]f_{2}) and not contained in t⋅(ℂ⁡[[t]]​f1+ℂ⁡[[t]]​f2)t\cdot(\mathbb{C}[[t]]f_{1}+\mathbb{C}[[t]]f_{2}). If Λ=ℂ⁡[[t]]​f1+ℂ⁡[[t]]​f2\Lambda=\mathbb{C}[[t]]f_{1}+\mathbb{C}[[t]]f_{2}, then we are finished. If not we consider the invariant lattice Λ+t⋅(ℂ⁡[[t]]​f1+ℂ⁡[[t]]​f2)\Lambda+t\cdot(\mathbb{C}[[t]]f_{1}+\mathbb{C}[[t]]f_{2}). Since Δ\Delta induces on (ℂ⁡[[t]]​f1+ℂ⁡[[t]]​f2)/t⋅(ℂ⁡[[t]]​f1+ℂ⁡[[t]]​f2)(\mathbb{C}[[t]]f_{1}+\mathbb{C}[[t]]f_{2})/t\cdot(\mathbb{C}[[t]]f_{1}+\mathbb{C}[[t]]f_{2}) a nilpotent map with only one proper invariant subspace, namely generated by the image of f2f_{2}, we have that Λ+t⋅(ℂ⁡[[t]]​f1+ℂ⁡[[t]]​f2)=(ℂ⁡[[t]]​t​f1+ℂ⁡[[t]]​f2)\Lambda+t\cdot(\mathbb{C}[[t]]f_{1}+\mathbb{C}[[t]]f_{2})=(\mathbb{C}[[t]]tf_{1}+\mathbb{C}[[t]]f_{2}). It follows that Λ\Lambda contains an element of the form a​f1+f2af_{1}+f_{2} for some a∈t​ℂ​[[t]]a\in t\mathbb{C}[[t]]. Now

Δ⁡(a​f1+f2)−(a+12​h)​(a​f1+f2)=(t+h−1​t​d​ad​t−(a+12​h)​a)​f1∈Λ.\Delta(af_{1}+f_{2})-(a+\frac{1}{2h})(af_{1}+f_{2})=(t+h^{-1}t\frac{da}{dt}-(a+\frac{1}{2h})a)f_{1}\in\Lambda.

Thus t​f1∈Λtf_{1}\in\Lambda and also f2∈Λf_{2}\in\Lambda. Then Λ=ℂ⁡[[t]]​t​f1+ℂ⁡[[t]]​f2\Lambda=\mathbb{C}[[t]]tf_{1}+\mathbb{C}[[t]]f_{2}.

Comment. Two lattices Λ1,Λ2\Lambda_{1},\Lambda_{2} in ℂ​((t))2\mathbb{C}((t))^{2} are called equivalent if there exists an integer nn with Λ1=tn⋅Λ2\Lambda_{1}=t^{n}\cdot\Lambda_{2}. Two classes of lattices [Λ1],[Λ2][\Lambda_{1}],\ [\Lambda_{2}] form an edge if the representatives Λ1,Λ2\Lambda_{1},\Lambda_{2} can be chosen such that there are proper inclusions t⋅Λ1⊂Λ2⊂Λ1t\cdot\Lambda_{1}\subset\Lambda_{2}\subset\Lambda_{1}. One obtains a tree with vertices the classes of lattices and edges as above. If one replaces ℂ\mathbb{C} by a finite field then this object is the well known Bruhat-Tits tree.

The classes of the invariant lattices form a subset of this tree. This subset is a line for the first case of (i) and a half line for the second case of (i). In case (ii), it is again a line and in case (iii) this subset consists of two vertices which form an edge. □\Box

1.3. The analytic classification

This is the classification of the differential modules MM over the field of the convergent Laurent series ℂ⁡({t})\mathbb{C}(\{t\}). Again we use the derivation t​dd​tt\frac{d}{dt}. One associates to MM the formal differential module M^=ℂ⁡((t))⊗M\widehat{M}=\mathbb{C}((t))\otimes M. If M^\widehat{M} is regular singular, then one calls MM also regular singular. In that case there exists also a basis e1,…,ede_{1},\dots,e_{d} of MM such that W:=⊕i=1dℂeiW:=\oplus_{i=1}^{d}\mathbb{C}e_{i} is invariant under δ\delta and the distinct eigenvalues of the matrix AA of δ\delta on WW do not differ by an integer. Then MM is isomorphic to the module corresponding to the matrix differential operator t​dd​t+At\frac{d}{dt}+A. The usual topological monodromy around t=0t=0 coincides with the formal monodromy and that ends the classification.

If M^\widehat{M} is irregular singular, then it induces a tuple (V,{Vq},γ)(V,\{V_{q}\},\gamma). The singular directions d∈ℝd\in\mathbb{R} of MM depend only on M^\widehat{M} and are defined as follows. Let q1,…,qsq_{1},\dots,q_{s} denote the eigenvalues of M^\widehat{M}. A direction d∈ℝd\in\mathbb{R} is singular for qi−qjq_{i}-q_{j} (with i≠ji\neq j) if the function e​x​p​(∫(qi−qj)​d​tt)exp(\int(q_{i}-q_{j})\frac{dt}{t}) has maximal descent for r→0r\rightarrow 0 on the half line t=r​ei​dt=re^{id}. The collection of the singular directions is the union over i≠ji\neq j of the singular directions of qi−qjq_{i}-q_{j}.

If a direction dd is non singular, then there is a functorial map m​u​l​t​sdmults_{d}, the multisummation in the direction dd, which maps the (symbolic) solution space VV to the space of the actual solutions V⁡(S)V(S) in a certain sector SS at t=0t=0 around dd. For every v∈Vv\in V the element m​u​l​t​sd​(v)mults_{d}(v) has vv as its asymptotic expansion.

For each singular direction dd, there is an analytic object, namely the Stokes map S​td∈GL⁡(V)St_{d}\in{\rm GL}(V). The Stokes map S​tdSt_{d} is defined by comparing the multisummation at directions d−<d<d+d^{-}<d<d^{+} close to dd. More precisely m​u​l​t​sd+∘S​td=m​u​l​t​sd−mults_{d^{+}}\circ St_{d}=mults_{d^{-}}. The map S​tdSt_{d} is unipotent and has the form I​d+∑i,jLi,jId+\sum_{i,j}L_{i,j} where the sum is taking over all pairs i,ji,j such that dd is singular for qi−qjq_{i}-q_{j} and where Li​jL_{ij} is a linear map from VqiV_{q_{i}} to VqjV_{q_{j}}. The isomorphy class of MM induces a tuple (V,{Vq},γ,{S​td})(V,\{V_{q}\},\gamma,\{St_{d}\}), where the S​tdSt_{d} are described above and where moreover the relation γ−1​S​td​γ=S​td+2​π\gamma^{-1}St_{d}\gamma=St_{d+2\pi} holds.
The main result of the asymptotic analysis of irregular singularities is:

The category of the differential modules over ℂ⁡({t})\mathbb{C}(\{t\}) is equivalent to the category of the tuples (V,{Vq},γ,{S​td})(V,\{V_{q}\},\gamma,\{St_{d}\}), satisfying the above properties. This equivalence respects all constructions of linear algebra, in particular the tensor product.

An important property that we will use is:

Let 0≤d1<⋯<ds<2​π0\leq d_{1}<\dots<d_{s}<2\pi denote the singular directions in [0,2​π)[0,2\pi). Then the topological monodromy around the singular point is conjugated to γ∘Stdr∘⋯∘Std1\gamma\circ St_{d_{r}}\circ\cdots\circ St_{d_{1}}.

We note that this conjugation depends on the way the solution space at a point close to the singular point t=0t=0 is identified with the (formal) solution space VV. Now we illustrate the above by continuing Examples 1.1.

1.4. The data for global differential modules

By a global differential module we mean a differential module MM over the field K=ℂ⁡(z)K=\mathbb{C}(z). We investigate the data that will describe MM.
The first case that we consider is classical, namely:
The position of the singular points {p1,…,pr}\{p_{1},\dots,p_{r}\} of MM is fixed and all the singular points are supposed to be regular singular.

One introduces the monodromy for MM in the usual way. That is, one chooses a base point b∈ℙ1∖{p1,…,pr}b\in\mathbb{P}^{1}\setminus\{p_{1},\dots,p_{r}\} and loops α1,…,αr\alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{r} around the singular points, generating the fundamental group π1:=π1​(ℙ1∖{p1,…,pr},b)\pi_{1}:=\pi_{1}(\mathbb{P}^{1}\setminus\{p_{1},\dots,p_{r}\},b). There is only one relation, namely α1⋯αr=1\alpha_{1}\cdots\alpha_{r}=1. Then MM induces a monodromy homomorphism

m​o​nM:π1→GL⁡(V⁡(b)),mon_{M}:\pi_{1}\rightarrow{\rm GL}(V(b))\ ,

where V⁡(b)V(b) denotes the solution space at bb. We note that m​o​nM​(αi)mon_{M}(\alpha_{i}) is conjugated to the local monodromy at pip_{i} (formal or topological). A weak solution of the Riemann–Hilbert problem reads ([PS],Thm 6.15):

Proposition 1.4.

The functor M↦m​o​nMM\mapsto mon_{M} from the category of the differential modules with regular singularities at {p1,…,pr}\{p_{1},\dots,p_{r}\} to the category of the finite dimensional complex representations of π\pi, is an equivalence of categories. This equivalence respects all constructions of linear algebra, in particular tensor products.

Notation. For any point p∈ℙ1p\in\mathbb{P}^{1} we introduce the local parameter tpt_{p}, which is z−pz-p if p∈ℂp\in\mathbb{C} and z−1z^{-1} for p=∞p=\infty. The field KpK_{p} is the field of the meromorphic functions at pp, i.e., ℂ⁡({tp})\mathbb{C}(\{t_{p}\}) and K^p\widehat{K}_{p} is the completion of KpK_{p}, i.e., ℂ⁡((tp))\mathbb{C}((t_{p})). Further Op⊂KpO_{p}\subset K_{p} and O^p⊂K^p\widehat{O}_{p}\subset\widehat{K}_{p} are the valuation rings, i.e., Op=ℂ​{tp}O_{p}=\mathbb{C}\{t_{p}\} and O^p=ℂ⁡[[tp]]\widehat{O}_{p}=\mathbb{C}[[t_{p}]].

One associates to a global differential module MM with fixed singularities {p1,…,pr}\{p_{1},\dots,p_{r}\}, the data: the isomorphy classes of the {Kpi⊗KM}\{K_{p_{i}}\otimes_{K}M\} and the monodromy representation m​o​nMmon_{M} as above. Now we give an example showing that this is not sufficient for the reconstruction of MM.

Example 1.5.

Two singular points 00 and ∞\infty, both irregular.
At both points we prescribe local analytic data for the differential module MM. In other words, we prescribe the two analytic differential modules M0=K0⊗MM_{0}=K_{0}\otimes M and M∞=K∞⊗MM_{\infty}=K_{\infty}\otimes M. As we will see in Observations 1.8, this leads to a connection (ℳ,∇)(\mathcal{M},\nabla) on ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}, where ℳ\mathcal{M} is a vector bundle and ∇:ℳ→Ω⁡(k⁡[0]+k⁡[∞])⊗ℳ\nabla:\mathcal{M}\rightarrow\Omega(k[0]+k[\infty])\otimes\mathcal{M} (for some k>0k>0). The restrictions T0T_{0} and T1T_{1} of this connection to the two open sets ℙ1∖{0}\mathbb{P}^{1}\setminus\{0\} and ℙ1∖{∞}\mathbb{P}^{1}\setminus\{\infty\} are known from the given data M0M_{0} and M∞M_{\infty}. We suppose now that the topological monodromies of M0M_{0} and M∞M_{\infty} are trivial. Thus the restrictions T0,1T_{0,1} and T1,0T_{1,0} of T0T_{0} and T1T_{1} to the open set ℙ1∖{0,∞}\mathbb{P}^{1}\setminus\{0,\infty\} are trivial. The glueing is given by an isomorphism T0,1→T1,0T_{0,1}\rightarrow T_{1,0}. Let mm denote the dimension of MM. Then an isomorphism is given by a linear bijection L:ℂm→ℂmL:\mathbb{C}^{m}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}^{m}. Further LL is unique up to multiplication (on the left, respectively on the right) by an automorphism of M0M_{0} and M∞M_{\infty}. One can easily produce M0M_{0} and M∞M_{\infty} which have only ℂ∗\mathbb{C}^{*} as group of automorphisms. Therefore the possible connections (ℳ,∇)(\mathcal{M},\nabla) and also the possible differential modules MM are in bijection with PGL⁡(m,ℂ){\rm PGL}(m,\mathbb{C}). □\Box

Definition 1.6.

Links and the formal and analytic data.
What is missing is a ‘link’ between the solution space V⁡(b)V(b) at the base point bb with the (symbolic) solution spaces V⁡(pi)V(p_{i}) at the singular points. We make the following construction to remedy this.

As before, α1,…,αr\alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{r} are loops starting at bb around the singular points. For each pip_{i} we choose a point pi∗p_{i}^{*} on the loop close to pip_{i} and a line segment [pi∗,pi][p_{i}^{*},p_{i}] which is a non–singular direction at pip_{i}. The ‘link’ Li:V⁡(b)→V⁡(pi)L_{i}:V(b)\rightarrow V(p_{i}) is defined by analytic continuation from V⁡(b)V(b) to V⁡(pi∗)V(p_{i}^{*}), followed by the inverse of the multisummation map m​u​l​t​s:V⁡(pi)→V⁡(pi∗)mults:V(p_{i})\rightarrow V(p_{i}^{*}) in the direction [pi∗,pi][p_{i}^{*},p_{i}] (seen as an element in ℝ\mathbb{R}). The role of the monodromy map m​o​nMmon_{M} is taken over by links, i.e., the linear bijections L1,…,LrL_{1},\dots,L_{r}. The multisummation m​u​l​t​s:V⁡(pi)→V⁡(pi∗)mults:V(p_{i})\rightarrow V(p_{i}^{*}) (in the direction [pi,pi∗][p_{i},p_{i}^{*}]) is used to identify the two vector spaces. Then the local topological monodromy t​o​pitop_{i}, along a circle starting in pi∗p_{i}^{*}, is expressed as a product of the Stokes maps and the formal monodromy at pip_{i}. The relation α1⋯αr=1\alpha_{1}\cdots\alpha_{r}=1 translates into

Lr−1∘t​o​pr∘Lr​…​L2−1∘t​o​p2∘L2∘L1−1∘t​o​p1∘L1=1.L_{r}^{-1}\circ top_{r}\circ L_{r}\dots L_{2}^{-1}\circ top_{2}\circ L_{2}\circ L_{1}^{-1}\circ top_{1}\circ L_{1}=1.

The ‘formal and the analytic data’ for MM are defined as:

  1. (1)

    The position of the singular points p1,…,prp_{1},\dots,p_{r};

  2. (2)

    for each ii, the formal structure (V⁡(pi),{V​(pi)q},γi)(V(p_{i}),\{V(p_{i})_{q}\},\gamma_{i}) at pip_{i};

  3. (3)

    for each ii, the Stokes maps at pip_{i};

  4. (4)

    the links Li:W→V⁡(pi)L_{i}:W\rightarrow V(p_{i}).

  5. (5)

    These data are supposed to satisfy the relation

    Lr−1∘t​o​pr∘Lr​…​L2−1∘t​o​p2∘L2∘L1−1∘t​o​p1∘L1=1.L_{r}^{-1}\circ top_{r}\circ L_{r}\dots L_{2}^{-1}\circ top_{2}\circ L_{2}\circ L_{1}^{-1}\circ top_{1}\circ L_{1}=1.

Here WW stands for the space V⁡(b)V(b). The formal part of the data is (1) (the position of the singular points) and the eigenvalues qq at each singular point. The analytic part of the data is the direct sum decompositions ⊕qV(pi)q\oplus_{q}V(p_{i})_{q} of the spaces V⁡(pi)V(p_{i}), including the permutation of the V​(pi)qV(p_{i})_{q} induced by γ\gamma; further (3) and (4), since this combines the links and the Stokes maps. We observe that these ‘formal and analytic data’ are considered up to the automorphisms of WW and of the V⁡(pi)V(p_{i}).

One might use L1L_{1} to identify WW with V⁡(p1)V(p_{1}) and then one is only left with links Li:V⁡(p1)→V⁡(pi)L_{i}:V(p_{1})\rightarrow V(p_{i}) for i=2,…,ri=2,\dots,r. Another way to reduce the number of links by one, is to choose as base point bb the singular point p1p_{1} and define links Li:V⁡(p1)→V⁡(pi)L_{i}:V(p_{1})\rightarrow V(p_{i}) for i=2​…,ri=2\dots,r. □\Box

Theorem 1.7.

For given ‘formal and analytic data’, as above, there exists a differential module MM over K=ℂ⁡(z)K=\mathbb{C}(z) inducing the data. Moreover MM is unique up to isomorphism.

Observations 1.8.

Global differential modules and connections.
Before giving the proof of Theorem 1.7, we have to make the relation between differential modules MM over K=ℂ⁡(z)K=\mathbb{C}(z) and connections (ℳ,∇)(\mathcal{M},\nabla) (with singularities) on ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1} explicit.

Let a connection (ℳ,∇)(\mathcal{M},\nabla) (with singularities) be given. We note that we may regard this connection either algebraically or analytically, because of the GAGA theorem. On proper Zariski-open subsets of ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1} we sometimes see ℳ\mathcal{M} as an analytic vector bundle. The generic fibre MM of ℳ\mathcal{M} is a vector space of finite dimension over KK, equipped with a ∇:M→ΩK/ℂ⊗M\nabla:M\rightarrow\Omega_{K/\mathbb{C}}\otimes M. After identifying ΩK/ℂ\Omega_{K/\mathbb{C}} with K​d​zKdz, this gives MM the structure of a differential module.

On the other hand, let a differential module MM be given. This is written as a (generic) connection ∇:M→ΩK/ℂ⊗M\nabla:M\rightarrow\Omega_{K/\mathbb{C}}\otimes M. Consider a set {p1,…,pr}⊂ℙ1\{p_{1},\dots,p_{r}\}\subset\mathbb{P}^{1} of points including the singular points of MM. For each ii one chooses an O^pi\widehat{O}_{p_{i}}-lattice Λi\Lambda_{i} in K^pi⊗M\widehat{K}_{p_{i}}\otimes M and let kik_{i} satisfy ∇(Λi)⊂ti−ki​d​ti⊗Λi\nabla(\Lambda_{i})\subset t_{i}^{-k_{i}}dt_{i}\otimes\Lambda_{i} (where tit_{i} is the local parameter at pip_{i}). For p∉{p1,…,pr}p\not\in\{p_{1},\dots,p_{r}\}, the module K^p⊗M\widehat{K}_{p}\otimes M is non singular and there is a unique O^p\widehat{O}_{p}-lattice Λp\Lambda_{p} with ∇(Λp)⊂d​tp⊗Λp\nabla(\Lambda_{p})\subset dt_{p}\otimes\Lambda_{p}, where tpt_{p} denotes the local parameter at pp. Then there exists a unique connection (ℳ,∇)(\mathcal{M},\nabla) on ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1} having the following properties (see [PS], Lemma 6.16):

  1. (1)

    ℳ⁡(V)⊂M\mathcal{M}(V)\subset M for all, non empty, Zariski–open V⊂ℙ1V\subset\mathbb{P}^{1}.

  2. (2)

    There is a basis e1,…,eme_{1},\dots,e_{m} of MM and a non empty Zariski–open subset U⊂ℙ1U\subset\mathbb{P}^{1} such that the restriction of ℳ\mathcal{M} to UU is the free algebraic vector bundle OU​e1⊕⋯⊕OU​emO_{U}e_{1}\oplus\cdots\oplus O_{U}e_{m}.

  3. (3)

    For each pip_{i} one has ℳ^pi=Λi\widehat{\mathcal{M}}_{p_{i}}=\Lambda_{i}.

  4. (4)

    For p∉{p1,…,pr}p\not\in\{p_{1},\dots,p_{r}\} one has ℳ^p=Λp\widehat{\mathcal{M}}_{p}=\Lambda_{p}.

  5. (5)

    ∇:ℳ→Ω⁡(∑ki​[pi])⊗ℳ\nabla:\mathcal{M}\rightarrow\Omega(\sum k_{i}[p_{i}])\otimes\mathcal{M}.

We still need another ingredient for the proof of Theorem 1.7. Let a differential module NN over Kp=ℂ⁡({tp})K_{p}=\mathbb{C}(\{t_{p}\}) be given and be written in the form ∇:N→Kp​d​tp⊗N\nabla:N\rightarrow K_{p}dt_{p}\otimes N. Choose any ℂ​{tp}\mathbb{C}\{t_{p}\}-lattice Λ⊂N\Lambda\subset N and let k≥0k\geq 0 be such that ∇(Λ)⊂tp−k​d​tp⊗Λ\nabla(\Lambda)\subset t_{p}^{-k}dt_{p}\otimes\Lambda. Then the latter map extends to a connection (𝒩,∇)(\mathcal{N},\nabla), defined on a suitable small disk around pp and has the property ∇:𝒩→Ω⁡(k⁡[p])⊗𝒩\nabla:\mathcal{N}\rightarrow\Omega(k[p])\otimes\mathcal{N}. We note that this extension depends on the choice of the lattice Λ\Lambda or more precisely on the unique lattice Λ′\Lambda^{\prime} in ℂ⁡((tp))⊗N\mathbb{C}((t_{p}))\otimes N with Λ′∩N=Λ\Lambda^{\prime}\cap N=\Lambda. □\Box

Proof of Theorem 1.7. We use the notation of Definition 1.6. For r=0r=0, the data set is empty. The only module MM corresponding to this is the trivial differential module (of the required dimension, say mm).

For r=1r=1, the data at p1p_{1} determines a differential module M1M_{1} over Kp1K_{p_{1}}. We choose a lattice Λ⊂M1\Lambda\subset M_{1} (say the standard lattice) and then the connection ∇1:Λ→Ω⁡(k⋅[p1])⊗Λ\nabla_{1}:\Lambda\rightarrow\Omega(k\cdot[p_{1}])\otimes\Lambda (some k≥0k\geq 0) extends to a connection (ℳ1,∇1)(\mathcal{M}_{1},\nabla_{1}) on a small open disk DD around p1p_{1}. The topological monodromy around p1p_{1} of this connection is trivial. We consider the trivial connection (ℳ0,∇0)(\mathcal{M}_{0},\nabla_{0}) (of the required rank mm) on ℙ1∖{p1}\mathbb{P}^{1}\setminus\{p_{1}\}. The two connections can be glued over D∖{p1}D\setminus\{p_{1}\}, because of the triviality of t​o​p1top_{1}, and there results a connection (ℳ,∇)(\mathcal{M},\nabla) on ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}. Its generic fibre MM is a differential module over KK, inducing the given complete data.

Let NN be another differential module over KK inducing the given (formal and analytic) data. Then Kp1⊗NK_{p_{1}}\otimes N is isomorphic to Kp1⊗MK_{p_{1}}\otimes M and we choose in Kp1⊗NK_{p_{1}}\otimes N the lattice which maps to the lattice Λ⊂Kp1⊗M\Lambda\subset K_{p_{1}}\otimes M. This yields a connection (𝒩,∇N)(\mathcal{N},\nabla_{N}) with only p1p_{1} as singularity. Outside p1p_{1} the two connections are isomorphic and the same holds above a small enough disk DD around p1p_{1}. The two isomorphisms above D∖{p1}D\setminus\{p_{1}\} will differ by an element in GLm​(ℂ){\rm GL}_{m}(\mathbb{C}) (where m=dimMm=\dim M). The isomorphism between the connections above ℙ1∖{p1}\mathbb{P}^{1}\setminus\{p_{1}\} can be changed by any element in GLm​(ℂ){\rm GL}_{m}(\mathbb{C}). Then, after this change, the two connections are isomorphic and then NN is isomorphic to MM.

Now we suppose that r≥2r\geq 2. The monodromy determines a connection (ℳ0,∇0)(\mathcal{M}_{0},\nabla_{0}) on ℙ1∖{p1,…,pr}\mathbb{P}^{1}\setminus\{p_{1},\dots,p_{r}\}. The analytic data at pip_{i} determine a differential module over KpiK_{p_{i}}. For this differential module we choose the standard lattice as before. This extends to a connection (ℳi,∇i)(\mathcal{M}_{i},\nabla_{i}) on a small disk DiD_{i} around the point pip_{i}.

Since t​o​pitop_{i} is conjugated to the monodromy of the loop λi\lambda_{i}, we have that the restrictions of (ℳ0,∇0)(\mathcal{M}_{0},\nabla_{0}) and (ℳi,∇i)(\mathcal{M}_{i},\nabla_{i}) to Di∖{pi}D_{i}\setminus\{p_{i}\} are isomorphic. A priori, many isomorphisms are possible. However, the link LiL_{i} determines the isomorphism. Namely, one takes the isomorphism such that the map V⁡(b)→αV⁡(pi∗)→βV⁡(pi)V(b)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\alpha}}{{\rightarrow}}V(p_{i}^{*})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\beta}}{{\rightarrow}}V(p_{i}) is equal to the given LiL_{i}, where α\alpha is the analytic continuation for the connection (ℳ0,∇0)(\mathcal{M}_{0},\nabla_{0}) and β\beta is the inverse for the multisummation V⁡(pi)→V⁡(pi∗)V(p_{i})\rightarrow V(p_{i}^{*}) for the connection (ℳi,∇i)(\mathcal{M}_{i},\nabla_{i}). Glueing yields a connection (ℳ,∇)(\mathcal{M},\nabla) on ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1} and its generic fibre has the required properties.

Consider another differential module NN which produces the same (formal and analytic) data. Then NN yields a connection (𝒩,∇N)(\mathcal{N},\nabla_{N}). This connection is chosen such that the local connections at the points pip_{i} are standard, as above. This connection is, above ℙ1∖{p1,…,pr}\mathbb{P}^{1}\setminus\{p_{1},\dots,p_{r}\} and above each of the small enough disks DiD_{i}, isomorphic to the same items for (ℳ,∇)(\mathcal{M},\nabla). The links LiL_{i} imply that these isomorphisms glue to a global isomorphism between (𝒩,∇N)(\mathcal{N},\nabla_{N}) and (ℳ,∇)(\mathcal{M},\nabla), thus NN is isomorphic to MM. □\Box

Observations 1.9.

(1) In the construction in the proof of Theorem 1.7 from the given formal and analytic data to a connection (ℳ,∇)(\mathcal{M},\nabla) on ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}, one can change the lattices Λi\Lambda_{i} at the points pip_{i}. We note that this corresponds to an elementary transformation in [IIS1], Section 3. This will change the connection on ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}. However the corresponding differential module does not change.
(2) By Proposition 1.4, the links are superfluous in case all the singularities are regular singular. Another way to see this is to take the standard lattice at each point pip_{i}. Then the glueing of the connection (ℳ0,∇0)(\mathcal{M}_{0},\nabla_{0}) to the connection (ℳi,∇i)(\mathcal{M}_{i},\nabla_{i}) on a small disk DiD_{i} around pip_{i} is unique, since the connection (ℳi,∇i)(\mathcal{M}_{i},\nabla_{i}) on DiD_{i} and its restriction to Di∖{pi}D_{i}\setminus\{p_{i}\} have the same group of automorphisms, namely the elements in GL⁡(m,ℂ){\rm GL}(m,\mathbb{C}) commuting with the topological monodromy.
(3) Theorem 1.7 is the weak solution of the Riemann–Hilbert problem for differential modules with any type of singularities. □\Box

Definition and examples 1.10.

The strong Riemann-Hilbert problem.
This problem can be formulated as follows:
Let MM be the weak solution for the given formal and analytic data.
Does there exists a connection (ℳ,∇)(\mathcal{M},\nabla) with generic fibre MM and free vector bundle ℳ\mathcal{M} such that ∇:ℳ→Ω⁡(∑p(r+​(p)+1)​[p])⊗ℳ\nabla:\mathcal{M}\rightarrow\Omega(\sum_{p}(r^{+}(p)+1)[p])\otimes\mathcal{M}?
In the above, the sum ∑p\sum_{p} is taken over the singular points pp of MM, r⁡(p)r(p) is the Katz invariant of K^p⊗M\widehat{K}_{p}\otimes M and r+​(p)r^{+}(p) is the smallest integer ≥r⁡(p)\geq r(p).

One observes that in case that all the singularities are regular singular (this means that r⁡(p)=0r(p)=0 for every singular point pp) the above is the classical strong form of the Riemann–Hilbert problem.

In the proof of Theorem 1.7 one can choose at each singular point an invariant lattice which exists according to Definition and examples 1.2. One arrives at a connection (ℳ,∇)(\mathcal{M},\nabla) which satisfies all conditions with the exception that the vector bundle ℳ\mathcal{M} is possibly not free. Under the assumptions of Theorem 1.11, the invariant lattices can be changed to obtain a free vector bundle. Now we give two families of examples, closely related to the Painlevé equations, where the strong Riemann–Hilbert problem has a negative answer.

(1) The differential module MM is given by the matrix differential equation dd​z+(0​f1 0)\frac{d}{dz}+{0\ f\choose 1\ 0}, where f∈ℂ⁡[z]f\in\mathbb{C}[z] has degree 3. For MM there is no solution for the strong Riemann–Hilbert problem.

Proof.

The only singular point ∞\infty of MM has Katz invariant r=5/2r=5/2 and r+=3r^{+}=3. Suppose that MM can be represented by a connection (𝒱,∇)(\mathcal{V},\nabla) with 𝒱\mathcal{V} free and ∇:𝒱→Ω⁡(4​[∞])⊗𝒱\nabla:\mathcal{V}\rightarrow\Omega(4[\infty])\otimes\mathcal{V}. Write V=H0​(𝒱)V=H^{0}(\mathcal{V}). Then ∇:V→H0​(Ω⁡(4​[∞]))⊗V\nabla:V\rightarrow H^{0}(\Omega(4[\infty]))\otimes V and ∂:=∇dd​z\partial:=\nabla_{\frac{d}{dz}} has, with respect to a basis of VV, the form dd​z+B\frac{d}{dz}+B where BB is a polynomial matrix of degree ≤2\leq 2.

For computational convenience we may suppose that f=f3​z3+f1​z+f0f=f_{3}z^{3}+f_{1}z+f_{0} with f3≠0f_{3}\neq 0. There exists A∈GL2​(ℂ​(z))A\in{\rm GL}_{2}(\mathbb{C}(z)) with A−1​(dd​z+(0​f1 0))​A=dd​z+BA^{-1}(\frac{d}{dz}+{0\ f\choose 1\ 0})A=\frac{d}{dz}+B. One easily verifies that A∈GL2​(ℂ​[z])A\in{\rm GL}_{2}(\mathbb{C}[z]) and we may assume that AA has determinant 1. We use the notation (a​bc​d)t=(d−b−c​a){a\ b\choose c\ d}^{t}={d\ -b\choose-c\ a}. Theorem 1.11.

Suppose that the differential module MM over K=ℂ⁡(z)K=\mathbb{C}(z) is irreducible and has a (regular or irregular) singularity which is unramified. Then the strong Riemann-Hilbert problem has a solution for MM.

Proof.

We will adapt the proof of Theorem 6.22, [PS] to the present more general situation. As shown in the proof of Theorem 1.7, there exists a connection (ℳ,∇)(\mathcal{M},\nabla) such that ∇:ℳ→Ω⁡(∑(ki+1)​[pi])⊗ℳ\nabla:\mathcal{M}\rightarrow\Omega(\sum(k_{i}+1)[p_{i}])\otimes\mathcal{M}, where the pip_{i} are the singular points of MM and kik_{i} is the smallest integer ≥\geq the Katz invariant at pip_{i}. As in Proposition 6.21, [PS], the irreducibility of MM implies that the defect of any ℳ\mathcal{M} is bounded by a number only depending on MM.

Let p=p1p=p_{1} be an unramified singular point. Then we want to prove the equivalent of Lemma 6.20, [PS], namely for any integer N>1N>1, there exists a lattice Λ\Lambda for K^p⊗M\widehat{K}_{p}\otimes M such that Λ\Lambda has a basis e1,…,eme_{1},\dots,e_{m} with the property tp⋅∇ei=d​tp⊗((ci+ai)​ei+∑i≠jai,j​ej),t_{p}\cdot\nabla e_{i}=dt_{p}\otimes((c_{i}+a_{i})e_{i}+\sum_{i\neq j}a_{i,j}e_{j}), with ci∈ℂc_{i}\in\mathbb{C}; the ai∈tp−1​ℂ​[tp−1]a_{i}\in t_{p}^{-1}\mathbb{C}[t_{p}^{-1}] belong to the set of the eigenvalues of MM at pp and ai,j∈tpN​ℂ​[[tp]]a_{i,j}\in t_{p}^{N}\mathbb{C}[[t_{p}]].

It suffices to show the above for an indecomposable direct summand of K^p⊗M\widehat{K}_{p}\otimes M. This direct summand has only one eigenvalue and the formal monodromy γ\gamma has only one Jordan block. Then the proof of Lemma 6.20, [PS], yields the required lattice for this indecomposable direct summand.

Finally, as in the proof of Theorem 6.22, [PS], one can change the lattice Λ\Lambda step by step to obtain a connection (ℳ,∇)(\mathcal{M},\nabla) where ℳ\mathcal{M} has defect 0. Taking the tensor product with O⁡(k⁡[p1])O(k[p_{1}]) for a suitable kk makes ℳ\mathcal{M} free. ∎

2. Families of differential modules

2.1. Good families and the monodromy space ℛ\mathcal{R}

The aim is to study the formal and analytic data of a family of differential modules M⁡(u¯)M(\underline{u}) depending on some parameters u¯\underline{u}. Of course, this notion has to be made explicit. A rough approximation would be a matrix differential equation dd​z+A⁡(z,u¯)\frac{d}{dz}+A(z,\underline{u}) where each entry of the m×mm\times m-matrix A⁡(z,u¯)A(z,\underline{u}) is a rational function in zz with coefficients depending analytically on the parameters u¯\underline{u}. We recall that for a point pp, the local parameter is tpt_{p} (equal to z−pz-p or z−1z^{-1}). Further we use the notation of Subsection 1.2: V=V⁡(p)V=V(p) for the formal solution space at pp, the eigenvalues are q∗q_{*} and correspond to subspaces Vq∗V_{q_{*}} of VV. The singular directions at pp are defined in Subsection 1.3.

In order to have meaningful analytic data (as functions of u¯\underline{u}) one has to make some assumptions. A good family is defined by the properties:

  1. (1)

    The number rr of the singular points is fixed. The position of these points {p1,…,pr}\{p_{1},\dots,p_{r}\} may vary, but only slightly.

  2. (2)

    For every singular point pp, the degrees in tp−1t_{p}^{-1} of the eigenvalues qiq_{i} and the degrees in tp−1t_{p}^{-1} of the differences qi−qj,i≠jq_{i}-q_{j},\ i\neq j is fixed.

  3. (3)

    For every singular point pp and every eigenvalue qiq_{i}, the dimension of the space VqiV_{q_{i}} is fixed.

  4. (4)

    The top coefficients ci,jc_{i,j} of the qi−qjq_{i}-q_{j} may vary in a certain restricted way. Namely, we impose that any singular direction for the singular point pp is a singular direction for a unique difference qi−qj,i≠jq_{i}-q_{j},\ i\neq j of the eigenvalues at pp and that these singular directions vary slightly. As a consequence, the order of the directions at pp does not change in the family.

Comments 2.1.

 
(a) From (1) it follows that one can take a base point bb and loops α1,…,αr\alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{r} around the singular points, valid for all M⁡(u¯)M(\underline{u}). From a point pi∗p_{i}^{*} on λi\lambda_{i} and close to pip_{i}, the direction of the line segment [pi∗,pi][p_{i}^{*},p_{i}] is non singular and lies between the ‘same’ singular directions for the family M⁡(u¯)M(\underline{u}). This follows from (2), (3) and (4). Suppose that the family M⁡(u¯)M(\underline{u}) satisfies (1)–(3), and that for M⁡(0¯)M(\underline{0}) every singular direction of each singular point belongs to a unique difference qi−qj,i≠jq_{i}-q_{j},\ i\neq j of eigenvalues. Then condition (4) is valid for the restriction of this family to a suitable neighbourhood of u¯=0¯\underline{u}=\underline{0}.
(b) Let a differential module MM over K=ℂ⁡(z)K=\mathbb{C}(z) be given and assume that every singular direction of each singular point belongs to a unique difference of eigenvalues. We sketch the proof of the statement that there exists a local analytic family M⁡(u¯)M(\underline{u}), satisfying (1)–(4), such that M⁡(0¯)=MM(\underline{0})=M.

Write MM as a matrix differential equation dd​z+∑i=1r(∑n=1kiA⁡(i,n)(z−pi)n)\frac{d}{dz}+\sum_{i=1}^{r}(\sum_{n=1}^{k_{i}}\frac{A(i,n)}{(z-p_{i})^{n}}), with constant matrices A⁡(i,n)A(i,n). The subfamily dd​z+A⁡(z,u¯),u¯∈U\frac{d}{dz}+A(z,\underline{u}),\ \underline{u}\in U satisfying conditions (1)–(3), has the form U=D∩W≠∅U=D\cap W\neq\emptyset, where W⊂ℂNW\subset\mathbb{C}^{N} is a Zariski closed subset. (c) The statement in (b) justifies the naive way of writing a family, satisfying (1)–(4), locally as dd​z+A⁡(z,u¯)\frac{d}{dz}+A(z,\underline{u}). As mentioned in the introduction, the theory of Okamoto–Painlevé pairs has the aim to improve on this. In this paper however, we will deal with the naive local situation. □\Box

Let A​n​a​l​y​t​i​c​D​a​t​aAnalyticData denote the set of all tuples. This has a natural structure of an affine variety over ℂ\mathbb{C}. Two tuples ({γj},{Lj},{S​tk​(j)})(\{\gamma_{j}\},\{L_{j}\},\{St_{k}(j)\}) and ({γj′},{Lj′},{S​tk​(j)′})(\{\gamma_{j}^{\prime}\},\{L_{j}^{\prime}\},\{St_{k}(j)^{\prime}\}) are called equivalent, if there exists σj∈GL(V(j)),j=1,…,r,σ∈GL(W)\sigma_{j}\in{\rm GL}(V(j)),\ j=1,\dots,r,\ \sigma\in{\rm GL}(W) such that each σj\sigma_{j} preserves the direct sum decomposition ⊕V⁡(j,i)\oplus V(j,i) and further σj∘Lj=Lj′∘σ,j=1,…,r\sigma_{j}\circ L_{j}=L_{j}^{\prime}\circ\sigma,\ j=1,\dots,r and σj∘γj=γj′∘σj,j=1,…,r\sigma_{j}\circ\gamma_{j}=\gamma_{j}^{\prime}\circ\sigma_{j},\ j=1,\dots,r. In other words, the equivalence relation on A​n​a​l​y​t​i​c​D​a​t​aAnalyticData is given by the action of the reductive linear group algebraic group G:=GL⁡(W)×∏j,iGL⁡(V⁡(j,i))G:={\rm GL}(W)\times\prod_{j,i}{\rm GL}(V(j,i)).

The monodromy space ℛ\mathcal{R} is by definition AnalyticData//GAnalyticData//G, the categorical quotient. This is again an affine variety. In general this quotient is not a geometric one. In particular, a closed point of ℛ\mathcal{R} can correspond to many equivalence classes. One may use L1L_{1} to identify each space V⁡(1)V(1) with WW to reduce the space A​n​a​l​y​t​i​c​D​a​t​aAnalyticData and the group GG acting on it.

The map, which associates to u¯\underline{u} in DD (a small polydisk around 0¯\underline{0}) the tuple ({γj},{Lj},{S​tk​(j)})(\{\gamma_{j}\},\{L_{j}\},\{St_{k}(j)\}), is analytic. Indeed, it is rather clear that analytic continuation depends in an analytic way on u¯\underline{u}. That the same is valid for multisummation follows from [PS], Proposition 12.20, p. 314. Thus D→A​n​a​l​y​t​i​c​D​a​t​aD\rightarrow AnalyticData is analytic and hence D→ℛ:=AnalyticData//GD\rightarrow\mathcal{R}:=AnalyticData//G is analytic. The next example illustrates the above for a relatively simple case.

Remarks 2.3.

The papers of M. Jimbo, T. Miwa and K. Ueno.
The above introduction of families of differential modules and their formal and analytic data can be seen as an extension of the papers [JMU], [JM], which we will describe now, using our terminology.

In [JMU], [JM] the base point bb is taken to be ∞\infty and this point is supposed to be (irregular) singular. Further the irregular singularities pp are of a simple kind, namely all the eigenvalues (generalized exponents) qiq_{i} are in tp−1​ℂ​[tp−1]t_{p}^{-1}\mathbb{C}[t_{p}^{-1}], and all qiq_{i} and qi−qjq_{i}-q_{j} for i≠ji\neq j have the same degree in tp−1t_{p}^{-1} (there is one exception, related to the Painlevé I equation). We note that Example 2.2 is of the type considered in [JMU]. In particular, Borel summation or, better, kk-summation is sufficient for the asymptotic analysis of the singularity. A theorem of Y. Sibuya [Sib] gives the required input from asymptotics. The ‘links’, that we defined, are present in their work and the family of linear differential equations is presented as a matrix differential equation dd​z+A⁡(z,u¯)\frac{d}{dz}+A(z,\underline{u}). The origin of the examples, in the appendix of [JM], of families related to Painlevé I–VI, is probably classical (discovered by R. Fuchs [F], P. Painlevé [P], R. Garnier [Gar] et al.). Another source for similar examples are the ones discovered by H. Flaschka and A.C. Newell [FN]. Later work of B. Malgrange [Mal1, Mal2], clarifies and extends the papers [JMU], [JM].

The new tool ‘multisummation’ and the precise construction of the Stokes matrices, enables to generalize the work of Jimbo, Miwa and Ueno. Especially, as we will show in the next subsection, a ‘complete’ list of the equations related to Painlevé I–VI can be derived. Further, the monodromy spaces ℛ\mathcal{R} for the analytic data can now be computed and studied in detail. □\Box

2.2. Finding the list. Tables for connections and ℛ\mathcal{R}

We consider a local family M⁡(u¯)M(\underline{u}) of differential modules, represented by a matrix equation dd​z+A⁡(z,u¯)\frac{d}{dz}+A(z,\underline{u}) where A⁡(z,u¯)A(z,\underline{u}) is a 2×22\times 2-matrix with trace 0 and u¯\underline{u} lies in a small polydisk DD around 0¯\underline{0}. The possibilities of the formal structure at the singular points is given in Examples 1.1. The local Riemann–Hilbert map R​H:D→ℛRH:D\rightarrow\mathcal{R} forgets the formal data, namely the position of the set of singular points SS and the coefficients of the eigenvalues at the irregular singular points.

The position of the points SS contributes to the fibre, because of the automorphisms of ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}, the dimension max⁡(−3+#​S,0)\max(-3+\#S,0). A singular point pp with Katz invariant r⁡(p)r(p) contributes to the fiber the dimension r⁡(p)r(p) if r⁡(p)∈ℤ≥0r(p)\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0} and r+​(p)=12+r⁡(p)r^{+}(p)=\frac{1}{2}+r(p) if r⁡(p)∈12+ℤ≥0r(p)\in\frac{1}{2}+\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}. Further, in the space DD one divides by the action of a subgroup of the automorphisms of ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}.
The requirement that the fibres of R​HRH have dimension 1 produces the list:
#​S>4\#S>4 is excluded.
#​S=4\#S=4, then S={0,1,∞,t}S=\{0,1,\infty,t\}, only regular singular points, i.e., all r⁡(p)=0r(p)=0.
#​S=3\#S=3, then S={0,1,∞}S=\{0,1,\infty\} and only one irregular point with r⁡(p)∈{1,12}r(p)\in\{1,\frac{1}{2}\}. #​S=2\#S=2, then S={0,∞}S=\{0,\infty\}, the contribution of the singular points to the dimension of the fibre is 2, since we divide by the group z↦a​zz\mapsto az.
#​S=1\#S=1, then S={∞}S=\{\infty\}, the contribution of the singular point to the dimension of the fibre is 3, since we divide by the group z↦a​z+bz\mapsto az+b.

Columns 3–6 of the next table present the ten resulting cases. In the second column one finds the classification of the related Painlevé equation (some classes are divided into subclasses). The first column gives the extended Dynkin diagram of the corresponding Okamoto–Painlevé pair (see the Introduction). The space ℛ\mathcal{R} is mapped to a space of parameters 𝒫\mathcal{P} (related to the parameters spaces of the Painlevé equations) consisting of traces or eigenvalues of the matrices involved in the construction of ℛ\mathcal{R}.

We will not number these ten families, but indicate them by their Katz invariants, e.g., (0,0,0,0),(0,0,1),…,(0,−,3/2),(−,−,3),(−,−,5/2)(0,0,0,0),\ (0,0,1),\dots,\ (0,-,3/2),\ (-,-,3),\ (-,-,5/2). For a differential module MM corresponding to one of the types, the strong Hilbert-Riemann problem has a positive answer, except possibly for (1/2,−,1/2)(1/2,-,1/2) and (−,−,5/2)(-,-,5/2) (see Definitions and examples 1.10). For these two types we only consider the modules M⁡(u¯)M(\underline{u}) for which the strong Riemann–Hilbert problem does have a positive answer. The strong Riemann-Hilbert problem for a family M⁡(u¯)M(\underline{u}) is more subtle. It seems that connections on the vector bundle O⊕O⁡(−1)O\oplus O(-1) is better adapted to families. For the Painlevé VI case this is type of vector bundle is considered in [IIS1, IIS2]. Here however we will represent a family M⁡(u¯)M(\underline{u}) by connections on O⊕OO\oplus O. This defines, in general, an affine Zariski open subset of the space of all connections. However, the monodromy space ℛ\mathcal{R} classifies the analytic data (modulo some equivalence) for the complete space of all connections. For each type there are many possibilities. We will make choices that are helpful for the computation of the Painlevé equations and are moreover close to classical formulas.

It turns out that ℛ→𝒫\mathcal{R}\rightarrow\mathcal{P} is a family of affine cubic surfaces. There are two sources for the singularities of the fibres. The first one is reducibility of systems and is connected with the singularities of ℛ\mathcal{R} itself. The other source is resonance, i.e., at least one of the matrices involved in the construction of ℛ\mathcal{R} has a difference of eigenvalues belonging to ℤ∖{0}\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\}. Section 3 provides the computations of the families ℛ→𝒫\mathcal{R}\rightarrow\mathcal{P}. We will also describe the corresponding one-dimensional families of differential modules M⁡(t)M(t). This subsection ends with a list indicating the families of connections and presenting the families ℛ→𝒫\mathcal{R}\rightarrow\mathcal{P} of affine cubic surfaces by an equation. The monodromy space ℛ\mathcal{R} for (0,0,0,0)(0,0,0,0) is classical(cf.[FK, Iw1]), the others seem to be new. (See Table 2).

3. Computation of the monodromy spaces

3.1. Family (0,0,0,0)(0,0,0,0) and Painlevé VI

For completeness we describe this classical family. The family of differential modules is represented by dd​z+A⁡(z,t):=dd​z+A0z+A1z−1+Atz−t\frac{d}{dz}+A(z,t):=\frac{d}{dz}+\frac{A_{0}}{z}+\frac{A_{1}}{z-1}+\frac{A_{t}}{z-t} with constant 2×22\times 2 matrices having trace 0. Dividing by the action, by conjugation, of PSL2{\rm PSL}_{2} one finds a moduli space ℳ\mathcal{M} (say the categorical quotient) of differential modules with dimension 77.

The monodromy data are given by the tuples (B1,B2,B3,B4)∈SL24(B_{1},B_{2},B_{3},B_{4})\in{\rm SL}_{2}^{4} satisfying B1⋯B4=1B_{1}\cdots B_{4}=1. This defines an affine space of dimension 9. The categorical quotient ℛ\mathcal{R} of this space under the action, by conjugation with PSL2{\rm PSL}_{2}, has dimension 6. The fibres of R​H:ℳ→ℛRH:\mathcal{M}\rightarrow\mathcal{R} are parametrized by t∈ℙ1∖{0,1,∞}t\in\mathbb{P}^{1}\setminus\{0,1,\infty\}. For an isomonodromy family dd​z+A⁡(z,t)\frac{d}{dz}+A(z,t), the upper right entry of the matrix A⁡(z,t)A(z,t) has a single zero q=q⁡(t)q=q(t), which is the apparent singularity corresponding to the cyclic vector (01){0\choose 1}. Then qq is a solution of Painlevé VI. The matrix BB (of Subsection 4.1) has the form B0​(t)z−t\frac{B_{0}(t)}{z-t}. The computation of the equation for qq is classical (e.g., [F], [O2]).

The coordinate ring of ℛ\mathcal{R} is generated over ℂ\mathbb{C} by x1,x2,x3,a1,a2,a3,a4x_{1},x_{2},x_{3},a_{1},a_{2},a_{3},a_{4} with ai=t​r​(Bi)a_{i}=tr(B_{i}) and x1=t​r​(B2​B3),x2=t​r​(B1​B3),x3=t​r​(B1​B2)x_{1}=tr(B_{2}B_{3}),\ x_{2}=tr(B_{1}B_{3}),\ x_{3}=tr(B_{1}B_{2}). There is only one relation ([FK, Iw2]), namely (as in the list)

3.2. Family (0,0,1)(0,0,1) and Painlevé V

For a differential module of type (0,0,1)(0,0,1), the strong Riemann-Hilbert problem has a positive answer. Indeed, the lattices at 00 and 11 can be chosen arbitrary. By tradition one supposes that the corresponding local exponents are ±θ0/2\pm\theta_{0}/2 and ±θ1/2\pm\theta_{1}/2. From Definition and examples 1.2 one concludes that there exists a unique lattice at ∞\infty leading to a free vector bundle. By tradition, the generalized local exponents at ∞\infty are ±(tz+θ∞)/2\pm(tz+\theta_{\infty})/2. The module is then represented by the matrix differential equation dd​z+A0z+A1z−1+A∞\frac{d}{dz}+\frac{A_{0}}{z}+\frac{A_{1}}{z-1}+A_{\infty}, for certain constant matrices A0,A1,A∞A_{0},A_{1},A_{\infty} with trace 0. 4. The Painlevé equations

4.1. Finding the Painlevé equations

For each of the ten families of Section 3, with the exception of (0,0,0,0)(0,0,0,0), which is the well known classical case leading to PVI, we want to derive a corresponding Painlevé equation q′′=R⁡(q,q′,t)q^{\prime\prime}=R(q,q^{\prime},t).

We choose one of the other nine cases. A Zariski open part ℳ0\mathcal{M}^{0} of the corresponding moduli space is represented by a suitable matrix differential operator. Recall that there is a morphism p​r:ℳ0→T×Λpr:\mathcal{M}^{0}\rightarrow T\times\Lambda, where TT denotes the space of the ‘time variable’ tt and the parameter space Λ\Lambda consists of the local exponents for the regular singular points and the constant term of the generalized local exponents at the irregular singular points.

Choose λ∈Λ\lambda\in\Lambda, let a∈𝒫a\in\mathcal{P} be the image of λ\lambda in the parameter space of ℛ\mathcal{R}. Write ℳλ0=p​r−1​(T×{λ})\mathcal{M}^{0}_{\lambda}=pr^{-1}(T\times\{\lambda\}) and ℛa\mathcal{R}_{a} for the fibre of ℛ→𝒫\mathcal{R}\rightarrow\mathcal{P} at aa. Then the Riemann–Hilbert map restricts to R​Hλ:ℳλ0→ℛaRH_{\lambda}:\mathcal{M}^{0}_{\lambda}\rightarrow\mathcal{R}_{a} and the fibres of R​HλRH_{\lambda} are parametrized by tt. In particular, ℳλ0\mathcal{M}^{0}_{\lambda} has dimension 3. This space is represented by an explicit family of differential operators dd​z+A\frac{d}{dz}+A, where the entries of AA are rational functions in zz with coefficients depending on three explicit variables, say f,g,tf,g,t. Later on we will make a rather special choice for f,gf,g.

An isomonodromic family dd​z+A=dd​z+A⁡(z,t)\frac{d}{dz}+A=\frac{d}{dz}+A(z,t) on ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}, parametrized by tt, is a fibre of some R​HλRH_{\lambda}. The earlier variables f,gf,g are now functions of tt. Let SS denote the singular locus. On ℙ1∖S\mathbb{P}^{1}\setminus S there exists a multivalued fundamental matrix Y⁡(z,t)Y(z,t), i.e., (dd​z+A⁡(z,t))​Y​(z,t)=0(\frac{d}{dz}+A(z,t))Y(z,t)=0, normalized by detY⁡(z,t)=1\det Y(z,t)=1. By isomonodromy, dd​t​Y​(z,t)\frac{d}{dt}Y(z,t) and Y⁡(z,t)Y(z,t) have the same behaviour for Stokes and monodromy and thus B(z,t):=−dd​tY(z,t)⋅Y(z,t)−1B(z,t):=-\frac{d}{dt}Y(z,t)\cdot Y(z,t)^{-1} is univalued and extends in a meromorphic way at the set SS. Moreover B:=B⁡(z,t)B:=B(z,t) has trace 0 since detY⁡(z,t)=1\det Y(z,t)=1. Therefore the entries of BB are rational functions in zz and are analytic in tt. It follows that the operators dd​z+A⁡(z,t)\frac{d}{dz}+A(z,t) and dd​t+B⁡(z,t)\frac{d}{dt}+B(z,t) commute. This is equivalent to the identity

dd​t​A=dd​z​B+[B,A]​ and ​t​r​(B)=0.\frac{d}{dt}A=\frac{d}{dz}B+[B,A]\mbox{ and }tr(B)=0\ .

This equality is seen as a differential equation for matrices BB, rational in zz and with trace 0. Assume (as we will in the examples) that dd​z+A\frac{d}{dz}+A is irreducible, then BB is unique. Indeed, the difference CC of two solutions is rational in zz and satisfies dd​z​C=[C,A]\frac{d}{dz}C=[C,A]. Thus C⁡(dd​z+A)=(dd​z+A)​CC(\frac{d}{dz}+A)=(\frac{d}{dz}+A)C and CC is an endomorphism of dd​z+A\frac{d}{dz}+A. By irreduciblity, CC is a multiple of the identity and C=0C=0 because t​r​(C)=0tr(C)=0.

For the actual computation of BB for the cases of Subsection 2.2, the following remarks are useful. If z=cz=c is a regular, or regular singular point (without resonance), then BB has no pole at cc. If the Katz invariant r=r⁡(c)>0r=r(c)>0 is an integer, and the top coefficient of the eigenvalues at cc do not depend on tt, then o​r​dc​(B)≥−r+1ord_{c}(B)\geq-r+1. If however this top coefficient depends on tt, then o​r​dc​(B)≥−rord_{c}(B)\geq-r. If the Katz invariant r⁡(c)=m+12r(c)=m+\frac{1}{2} with integer m≥0m\geq 0, then o​r​dc​(B)≥−m−1ord_{c}(B)\geq-m-1. The above matrix equation yields explicit differential equations for f,gf,g as functions of tt, and an explicit BB.

The symbols p,qp,q denote a preferred choice for the variables f,gf,g. To define and find them we consider a pair (t,λ)∈T×Λ(t,\lambda)\in T\times\Lambda and the 2-dimensional space ℳt,λ0:=p​r−1​({(t,λ)}CLOSE\mathcal{M}^{0}_{t,\lambda}:=pr^{-1}(\{(t,\lambda)\}. Let dd​z+A\frac{d}{dz}+A be the corresponding matrix differential operator and let a cyclic vector ee be given. To make this explicit, suppose that A=(abc−a)A={a\ \ \ b\choose c\ -a} and that the first basis vector is the cyclic vector ee. Then

L=(dd​z)2−c′c⋅dd​z−a′−a2−b​c+a⋅c′c, where ​a′=d​ad​z​ etc.L=(\frac{d}{dz})^{2}-\frac{c^{\prime}}{c}\cdot\frac{d}{dz}-a^{\prime}-a^{2}-bc+a\cdot\frac{c^{\prime}}{c},\mbox{ where }a^{\prime}=\frac{da}{dz}\mbox{ etc.}

A Zariski open, dense part of the space ℳ(t,λ)0\mathcal{M}^{0}_{(t,\lambda)} is now parametrized by p,qp,q. On this space we introduce the symplectic structure by the closed 2-form d​p∧d​qF\frac{dp\wedge dq}{F} (with F∈{1,q,q2,q⁡(q−1)}F\in\{1,q,q^{2},q(q-1)\}) and thus p,qp,q are canonical coordinates. The Zariski open subset of the space ℳλ0\mathcal{M}^{0}_{\lambda} is parametrized by p,q,tp,q,t. This space has a foliation given by the isomonodromy families, i.e., the fibres of R​HλRH_{\lambda}. There is an Hamiltonian function H=H⁡(p,q,t)H=H(p,q,t), rational in p,qp,q and tt, such that this foliation coincides with the foliation deduced from the closed 2-form Ω=d​p∧d​qF−d​H∧d​t\Omega=\frac{dp\wedge dq}{F}-dH\wedge dt on ℳλ0\mathcal{M}^{0}_{\lambda}. Remarks 4.2.

(1) In general there are more complicated good cyclic vectors, than those in VV. However for (−,−,5/2)(-,-,5/2) there is only one good cyclic vector.
(2) If a cyclic vector v∈Vv\in V is eigenvector of two of the matrices, then the corresponding scalar equation has no apparent singularity. It is probable that another good cyclic vector yields a rational solution qq of the Painlevé equation.
(3) The good cyclic vectors, computed above, have a geometric meaning for the Okamoto–Painlevé pair.
(4) Most of the computations in this section were made using Mathematica.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
